claim: Calvin (Thomson and others 2012): a sequencing layer fixes one global order of transaction requests in each 10-millisecond epoch and locks are taken in that order, so every replica reaches the same state with no commit agreement.

Calvin (Thomson and others 2012), TPC-C New Order only on an EC2 cluster: about 5,000 transactions per second per node above 10 nodes, scaling linearly, and nearly half a million per second on 100 nodes; the baseline is a published Oracle record (504,161 per second on much higher-end hardware), not a controlled run; TPC-C has about 10 percent multi-warehouse transactions.

Calvin (Thomson and others 2012) compares with two-phase commit only by a model: the paper says the model of two-phase commit incurs significantly more slowdown than Calvin at very high contention; it is not a measurement.

Calvin (Thomson and others 2012), low contention, going from 1 machine to 4 or 8 machines: throughput falls about 5x to 7x, from 27,000 transactions per second to about 5,000 (4 nodes) or 4,000 (8 nodes); the paper names execution progress skew as the cause.

Calvin (Thomson and others 2012) needs every transaction's read and write sets before it starts; dependent transactions need a read-only reconnaissance query first and may restart if the reconnoitered set is no longer valid.

Harding and others 2017 (read via the library, not refetched): from two to four partitions performance drops 12 to 40 percent for protocols other than Calvin, and Calvin's throughput plummets when transactions touch more than one partition.

Harding and others 2017 (read via the library, not refetched): with data-dependent aborts Calvin fell 36 percent at theta 0.6 on 16 servers, and from 73k to 19k transactions per second between theta 0.8 and 0.9; on the PPS workload with reconnaissance queries Calvin flat-lined at about 7k transactions per second.

Abadi and Faleiro 2018 (CACM overview of deterministic database systems): three ways to run transactions concurrently while staying deterministic are partitioning (H-Store), locks requested in log order (Calvin) and dependency graphs (BOHM).
Abadi and Faleiro 2018: if transactions do not know their access sets in advance, they must run approximately serially with no concurrency whatsoever.

Abadi and Faleiro 2018: OLLP adds latency and cost, cannot be used with interactive transactions, and for interactive transactions the client must declare the access set or the system defaults to slow serial execution.
Abadi and Faleiro 2018, a figure they cite from another source (secondary citation, not measured here): log generation takes approximately 11 percent of all CPU cycles in non-deterministic engines.

Lu and others 2020 (Aria): transactions run in batches in parallel against one snapshot, writes are reserved by transaction id, and each transaction commits or aborts by a fixed rule; aborted transactions rerun in the next batch, and a fallback phase reruns conflicting ones Calvin style when the abort rate is high.

Lu and others 2020 (Aria), single node with 12 worker threads, YCSB 80/20 read/write, uniform access, batch of 1K: throughput 1.1x AriaFB, 1.6x BOHM, 1.4x PWV-A, 3.3x PWV-B, 2.4x Calvin and 10.3x PB (a primary-backup engine with strict two-phase locking and NO_WAIT); contention is low, abort rate about 0.4 percent.
Lu and others 2020 (Aria): at skew factor 0.999 the deterministic reordering rule gives 3.0x the throughput of Aria without it.

Lu and others 2020 (Aria): at skew factor 0.999 Aria reaches only 39 percent of its throughput with no skew, because many transactions have to be re-run several times; it falls below PWV-A above skew 0.8 and below BOHM above 0.9.

Lu and others 2020 (Aria), TPC-C subset on 180 partitions: 1.9x BOHM, 1.2x Calvin and 7.4x PB throughput, and comparable throughput to PWV; with few warehouses Aria is worse because of one contended write.

O'Neil 1986 (escrow method): the system keeps bounds inf(A) and sup(A), the lowest and highest values A may take from any combination of commits and aborts of live transactions; a request that keeps every test true is granted at once.

O'Neil 1986: waiting on a failed escrow test can bring deadlock, and detecting it is NP-complete (shown in a separate paper, as this paper states); the paper treats it as rare and handles it by heuristics such as timeout.

Narula and others 2014 (Doppel, phase reconciliation): for contended records each core applies one chosen commutative operation to its own slice during a split phase, slices are merged at reconciliation in time proportional to the number of cores, and reads of split data wait for the next joined phase.

Narula and others 2014 (Doppel): on an 80-core machine, mostly run on 20 cores, INCR1 with 100 percent of transactions incrementing one hot key gives Doppel 6.2x Atomic, 19x 2PL and 38x OCC; with little conflict it does not split and matches OCC.
Narula and others 2014 (Doppel): up to 38x conventional concurrency control on microbenchmarks and up to 3x on a larger application, at the cost of increased latency for some transactions.

Narula and others 2014 (Doppel), RUBiS-C auction at high contention (alpha 1.8): three times the throughput of OCC, where OCC spends roughly 67 percent of its time running StoreBid, much of it retrying aborted transactions.
Narula and others 2014 (Doppel), LIKE benchmark with skew: almost twice the throughput of OCC, paid for by read latency of up to 20 ms.

Narula and others 2014 (Doppel): contended updates must be programmed as commutative; an update written in a non-splittable way (explicit reads and writes) makes Doppel run those transactions serially, with far less parallel speedup.
Clements and others 2013 (scalable commutativity rule): whenever interface operations commute, they can be implemented in a way that scales.

Clements and others 2013, an operating-system result and not a database one: Linux scales for 68 percent of the 13,664 COMMUTER-generated tests; the sv6 kernel is conflict-free for 13,528 of them against 9,389 for Linux.

Clements and others 2013 (mail server): with non-commutative operations throughput collapses at a small number of cores, while the commutative APIs reach 7.5x scalability from 1 socket (10 cores) to 8 sockets (80 cores).
Clements and others 2013: at 80 cores fstat is 3.9x more expensive than on Linux.

Clements and others 2013: commutativity is judged per state and arguments (two open calls with O_CREAT and O_EXCL often do not commute), and the designer may change the interface so that operations commute (the O_ANYFD flag).
Clements and others 2013: commutativity suffices for conflict-free accesses but may not be necessary, and no correct implementation can be conflict-free across all histories.

Bailis and others 2014/2015 (invariant confluence): divergent but I-valid database states can be merged into a valid state, and coordination-free execution is possible if and only if the transaction is I-confluent with respect to the invariant I.

Bailis and others 2014/2015 (TPC-C and a microbenchmark, 200 servers): over 12.7 million TPC-C New-Order transactions per second, a 25-fold improvement over prior results; coordination-free execution over 12 million per second against about 1.1 million for the lock-based version, and distributed locking throughput drops by over three orders of magnitude.

Bailis and others 2014/2015: sequential per-district order IDs, AUTO_INCREMENT inserts, user-chosen uniqueness, foreign key deletes and counter decrements under a lower bound are not I-confluent; foreign key inserts, system-chosen unique values, counter increments under a lower bound and secondary index updates are.
Bailis and others 2014/2015: if invariants are incorrectly or incompletely specified, an I-confluent database system may violate application-level correctness.

Kallman and others 2008 (H-Store): each site is one single-threaded daemon on one core with its own data; transactions are pre-defined stored procedures; a single-sited transaction needs no undo log, no concurrency control and no communication beyond replication.

Yu and others 2014 (1000-core simulation, read via the library, not refetched): H-Store outperforms all other schemes up to 800 cores for single-partition transactions with uniform access, and does not scale with transactions accessing four or more partitions.
handles: four or more partitions no scale

claim: Kingsbury 2016 (Jepsen analysis of VoltDB 6.3, funded by VoltDB): updates on one partition are ordered by that partition's leader and multi-partition operations by a single cluster-wide initiator; multi-partition procedures pass sequentially through the MPI, and their throughput slowly drops as node count rises.

Kingsbury 2016 (VoltDB 6.3): VoltDB's internal benchmarks, as the analyst relays them, suggest multi-partition transactions are practically limited to a few hundred updates per second or tens of thousands of reads per second; this is the vendor's own figure (self-reported), not a measurement by the analyst.
Kingsbury 2016 (VoltDB 6.3): stored procedures must be deterministic, and a nondeterministic run is detected by hashing the resulting statements and the system shuts down.
Kingsbury 2016 (VoltDB 6.3): under partitions and recovery the analysis found stale reads, dirty reads and lost updates.

Stonebraker and others 2007 (H-Store, The End of an Architectural Era): shared-nothing main-memory sites run stored procedures, and TPC-C transaction classes made single-sited, sterile or one-shot by schema design achieve a valid execution with no controls.

Stonebraker and others 2007 (authors' own engine, one run, self-reported): H-Store ran 70,416 TPC-C transactions per second against 850 for a commercial RDBMS tuned for several days by a DBA, a factor of 82; dual-core 2.8 GHz, 4 GB memory, partial TPC-C with no think time and no high availability.

Stonebraker and others 2007 (authors' account, self-reported): the commercial system spent about two-thirds of its elapsed time in its logging system; logging off is estimated at about 2,500 transactions per second (an estimate, not a run), and concurrency control is named as the next bottleneck.
Stonebraker and others 2007: the top TPC-C result cited is about 133,000 total transactions per second on a 128-core shared-memory machine, against H-Store at 35,000 transactions per core.

VoltDB Technical Overview (vendor datasheet, no measurement): each single-threaded partition operates autonomously, eliminating the need for locking and latching, and for multi-partition transactions one engine coordinates the others' work plans.
